Every node in a Containerlab lab is a container, so every network operating system you want to use must exist as a
Docker image on the host first. How you get that image depends on the vendor. Some publish it in a public registry,
some give you a file to download with an account, and some only ship a virtual machine disk.

This part shows all four routes on Ubuntu, then runs a two-router lab to prove an image works. It assumes you finished
[Part 1](../01-install-containerlab/).

| Route | Typical images | Account needed | Command |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pull from a public registry | Linux hosts, FRRouting | No | `docker pull` |
| Import a vendor download | Arista cEOS | Free account | `docker import` |
| Load a vendor download | Cisco XRd | Cisco account with entitlement | `docker load` |
| Build from a VM disk (vrnetlab) | Cisco Catalyst 8000V, XRv 9000, Juniper vJunos, Nokia SR OS | Varies | `make` |

::: {.callout-important}
## The workshop labs use Cisco XRd
The routers in the labs of Parts 2 to 5 run Cisco IOS XR, as the XRd container image. The workshop cannot give you
this image: you get it from Cisco yourself (Route 3 below). You also need the free Alpine Linux image from Route 1.
The other two routes are here for reference, for when you build labs with other network operating systems.
:::

## Docker image basics

An image is named `repository:tag`, for example `ios-xr/xrd-control-plane:7.11.2`. The tag is usually the software
version. A topology file refers to an image by exactly this name, so pick clear names and keep them.

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| List images on the host | `docker images` |
| Give an image another name | `docker tag <old name> <new name>` |
| Remove an image | `docker rmi <name>` |
| Show disk used by images | `docker system df` |

When you deploy a lab, Containerlab uses the local image if it exists and tries to pull it from a registry if it does
not. Pulling only works for public images, so vendor images must be loaded before you deploy.

Network OS images are large. Allow 3–5 GB of disk per image, and check free space with `df -h /var/lib/docker`.

## Route 1: pull a public image (Alpine Linux)

Images in a public registry need no account: `docker pull` downloads them. The labs in Parts 3 to 5 use Alpine Linux,
a very small Linux image, for the hosts at the edge of the network:

```bash
docker pull alpine:3
docker images alpine
```

The image is about 13 MB. It has the basic network tools a lab host needs: `ip`, `ping` and `traceroute`.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Containerlab kind | `linux` |
| Login | none: open a shell with `docker exec` (Part 4) |
| Interface names in the topology | `eth1`, `eth2`, … |
| Memory per node | a few MB |

Open-source routing software such as [FRRouting](https://frrouting.org) is published in public registries too, and
is pulled the same way.

## Route 2: import a vendor download (Arista cEOS)

Arista's cEOS is free but needs an account:

1. Create an account at [arista.com](https://www.arista.com) and log in.
2. Go to **Support → Software Download**, open **cEOS-lab**, and download the 64-bit archive for your release, for
   example `cEOS64-lab-4.32.0F.tar.xz`.
3. Copy the file to the lab host and import it, naming the image after its release:

```bash
docker import cEOS64-lab-4.32.0F.tar.xz ceos:4.32.0F
docker images ceos
```

cEOS ships as a file system archive, not a saved image, which is why it uses `docker import` rather than
`docker load`.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Containerlab kind | `arista_ceos` |
| Login | `admin` / `admin` |
| Interface names in the topology | `eth1`, `eth2`, … |

Use cEOS 4.32.0F or later on current Ubuntu releases. Older releases need cgroups v1, which Ubuntu no longer uses by
default.

## Route 3: load a vendor download (Cisco XRd)

Cisco XRd runs IOS XR as a container, and it is the router used in the labs of this workshop. The **control-plane**
image is the one for labs; the vRouter image is for forwarding performance and needs more host setup.

### Get and load the image

1. Log in to [software.cisco.com](https://software.cisco.com) with a Cisco account that is entitled to XRd, and
   download the XRd control-plane archive for your release. If you are a student, ask your institution or instructor
   how to get access; Cisco decides who may download XRd.
2. Copy it to the lab host and unpack it. It contains the image file `xrd-control-plane-container-x64.dockerv1.tgz`
   and signature files:

   ```bash
   mkdir xrd && tar -xzf xrd-control-plane-container-x64.<release>.tgz -C xrd
   ls xrd
   ```

3. Load the image and note the name Docker prints on the `Loaded image:` line. The name differs between releases:

   ```bash
   docker load -i xrd/xrd-control-plane-container-x64.dockerv1.tgz
   ```

4. Give it a clear name that includes the release, and use that name in your topologies:

   ```bash
   docker tag <name from the Loaded image line> ios-xr/xrd-control-plane:7.11.2
   docker images ios-xr/xrd-control-plane
   ```

Allow about 3 GB of disk for the 7.11.2 image. `docker images` reports between 1.3 and 2.7 GB, depending on the Docker version.

The workshop labs name the image `ios-xr/xrd-control-plane:7.11.2`. If you have another release, tag it with its own
version and change the `image:` lines in the lab topology files to match.

### Prepare the host

XRd opens many file watches. Raise the Linux limits once, permanently:

```bash
sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-xrd.conf > /dev/null <<'EOF'
fs.inotify.max_user_instances=64000
fs.inotify.max_user_watches=131072
EOF
sudo sysctl --system
```

These values run a 15-router XRd lab on the workshop host. Cisco's
[xrd-tools](https://github.com/ios-xr/xrd-tools) repository has a `host-check` script that tests a host for XRd:
run `scripts/host-check -p xrd-control-plane -e docker` from a clone of it.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Containerlab kind | `cisco_xrd` |
| Login | `clab` / `clab@123` |
| Interface names in the topology | `Gi0-0-0-0`, `Gi0-0-0-1`, … (IOS XR `GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0`, …) |
| Memory per node | about 1.6 GB in the workshop labs; allow 2.5 GB for routers that run routing protocols |

The `clab` login is created by the configuration Containerlab generates for XRd. If you give an XRd node your own
`startup-config`, Containerlab uses your file instead, so include a user and SSH in it, or SSH to the node is refused:

```
username clab
 group root-lr
 group cisco-support
 secret clab@123
!
line default
 transport input ssh
!
ssh server v2
```

## Route 4: build an image from a VM disk (vrnetlab)

Many vendors only ship their virtual routers as VM disks, usually `.qcow2` files. [vrnetlab](https://containerlab.dev/manual/vrnetlab/)
wraps such a disk and a small QEMU virtual machine in a container image, so Containerlab can run it like any other
node. Use the [srl-labs fork](https://github.com/srl-labs/vrnetlab); images built with the original project do not
work with Containerlab.

### Check that the host can run VMs

vrnetlab needs hardware virtualization (KVM):

```bash
sudo apt install -y cpu-checker
kvm-ok
ls -l /dev/kvm
```

`kvm-ok` should report "KVM acceleration can be used". On a cloud VM this needs nested virtualization or a bare-metal
instance; Part 5 covers this for AWS.

### Build an image (example: Cisco Catalyst 8000V)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/srl-labs/vrnetlab.git
cd vrnetlab/cisco/c8000v
cp ~/Downloads/c8000v-universalk9.17.11.01a.qcow2 .
make docker-image
docker images | grep c8000v
```

Each platform has its own folder (`cisco/`, `juniper/`, `nokia/` and so on) and a README with its exact steps. The
image is named after the platform and the version in the disk's file name. Check the name with `docker images` and
use it in your topology.

| Setting (Catalyst 8000V) | Value |
|---|---|
| Containerlab kind | `cisco_c8000v` |
| Login | `admin` / `admin` |
| Resources per node | 1 vCPU and 4 GB by default |
| Boot time | about 5 minutes; watch with `docker logs -f <container>` |

VM-based nodes boot far more slowly and use more memory than native container images. Prefer a container image when
the vendor offers one.

## Test the image: a two-router XRd lab

The workshop repository has a lab with two XRd routers joined by one link. A small startup configuration gives each
router an address on the link, so you can prove the image works end to end.

```yaml
name: xrd-pair

topology:
  nodes:
    xrd1:
      kind: cisco_xrd
      image: ios-xr/xrd-control-plane:7.11.2
      startup-config: xrd1.cfg
    xrd2:
      kind: cisco_xrd
      image: ios-xr/xrd-control-plane:7.11.2
      startup-config: xrd2.cfg

  links:
    # Gi0-0-0-0 here is GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 inside the router.
    - endpoints: ["xrd1:Gi0-0-0-0", "xrd2:Gi0-0-0-0"]
```

See it drawn in the [topology viewer](https://graphs.dynanet.dev/topology?example=xrd).

`xrd1.cfg` is an IOS XR configuration that the router loads when it starts (`xrd2.cfg` is the same with `xrd2`,
`to xrd1` and `10.0.12.2`):

```
hostname xrd1
username clab
 group root-lr
 group cisco-support
 secret clab@123
!
line default
 transport input ssh
!
lldp
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
 description to xrd2
 ipv4 address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
!
ssh server v2
end
```

| Lines | What they do |
|---|---|
| `username clab` to `secret clab@123` | Create the login you use over SSH |
| `line default`, `transport input ssh` and `ssh server v2` | Turn on the SSH server |
| `lldp` | Lets the two routers discover each other |
| `interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0` | Puts an address on the link. The topology file calls this interface `Gi0-0-0-0` |

### Deploy

First update your copy of the workshop files from Part 1, then deploy:

```bash
cd ~/dynanet-dev && git pull
cd ~/dynanet-dev/clab-workshop/labs/02-images
containerlab deploy -t xrd-pair.clab.yml
```

The command finishes in a few seconds. It ends with a table listing `clab-xrd-pair-xrd1` and `clab-xrd-pair-xrd2`,
both `running`. IOS XR then needs about another minute to start and load its configuration, so wait a moment before
you log in.

### Verify

Log in to `xrd1`. The password is `clab@123`:

```bash
ssh clab@clab-xrd-pair-xrd1
```

You get the IOS XR prompt, `RP/0/RP0/CPU0:xrd1#`. Run each check:

| Step | Command (on xrd1) | You should see |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Software | `show version` | `Cisco IOS XR Software, Version 7.11.2` and `cisco XRd Control Plane` |
| 2. Link up | `show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0` | `GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 is up, line protocol is up` |
| 3. Address | `show ipv4 interface brief` | a row for `GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0` with `10.0.12.1`, `Up` and `Up` |
| 4. Neighbour | `show lldp neighbors` | a row with Device ID `xrd2` and Local Intf `GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0` |
| 5. Reachability | `ping 10.0.12.2 count 3` | `!!!` and `Success rate is 100 percent (3/3)` |

Leave the router with `exit`. If SSH answers `Connection refused` or `Connection timed out`, or a check fails
straight after the deploy, the router is still starting: wait 30 seconds and try again.

Or run all the checks at once from the lab folder:

```bash
./verify.sh
```

```
Checking lab xrd-pair
  PASS  xrd1 is running
  PASS  xrd2 is running
  PASS  xrd1 answers the CLI: IOS XR 7.11.2 LNT
  PASS  xrd1 GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 is up
  PASS  xrd2 GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0 is up
  PASS  xrd1 sees xrd2 as an LLDP neighbour
  PASS  xrd1 pings xrd2 (10.0.12.1 -> 10.0.12.2), 100% success

All checks passed.
```

The script waits for the routers to finish starting before it checks them. Any `FAIL` line says what is wrong; the
troubleshooting table below covers the usual causes.

### Remove the lab

```bash
containerlab destroy -t xrd-pair.clab.yml --cleanup
```

`--cleanup` also removes the lab folder `clab-xrd-pair`, where XRd keeps its files, so the next deploy starts fresh.

To try another image, change `kind`, `image` and the interface names to the values in that route's table, and remove
the `startup-config` lines: the two files are IOS XR configuration.

## Move images between hosts

To prepare several lab hosts, download a vendor image once, then copy it:

```bash
docker save ios-xr/xrd-control-plane:7.11.2 | gzip > xrd-7.11.2.tar.gz   # on the host that has it
scp xrd-7.11.2.tar.gz user@labhost:                                      # copy it
docker load -i xrd-7.11.2.tar.gz                                         # on the new host
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Vendor images are licensed software
Cisco XRd and Arista cEOS images are covered by their vendors' licence terms. Do not put them in a public Git
repository, a public registry or a shared download link. Each attendee downloads them with their own account, or the
instructor loads them onto hosts the training provides, as the licence allows. Git is the wrong place for images in
any case: GitHub rejects files larger than 100 MB.
:::

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| Deploy fails with `pull access denied` or `manifest unknown` | The image is not on the host and is not public. Load it first, and check the name in the topology matches `docker images` exactly, tag included |
| `docker load` reports `invalid tar header` | You passed the outer XRd archive. Unpack it first and load the `.dockerv1.tgz` file inside |
| `no space left on device` while loading | Free disk space: `docker system df`, then `docker image prune` to remove unused images |
| XRd node restarts or logs inotify errors | The sysctl limits are not applied. Check with `sysctl fs.inotify.max_user_instances` |
| SSH to an XRd node answers `Connection refused` or `Connection timed out` just after a deploy | IOS XR is still starting. Wait a minute and try again |
| SSH to an XRd node is refused although it has booted | Your own `startup-config` has no user or `ssh server v2`. Add them (see Route 3) and redeploy with `--reconfigure` |
| `Connection closed` when you open SSH sessions to one router quickly, one after another | IOS XR limits how fast new SSH sessions may start. Wait two seconds between them |
| `rm -rf clab-<lab>` fails with `Permission denied` | XRd writes files owned by root into the lab folder. Remove the lab with `containerlab destroy --cleanup`, or use `sudo rm -rf clab-<lab>` |
| vrnetlab node never finishes booting | KVM is missing. Check `kvm-ok`, and on a VM enable nested virtualization |
